claims.text: FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be represented initially as a random solid solution.
Enhanced molecular dynamics using Umbrella Sampling or Metadynamics can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Free-energy barriers for transformations in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles depend on particle size.
Relevant thermal-stability simulations should span temperatures from ambient conditions to near melting.
Simulating multiple nanoparticle sizes captures finite-size effects in thermal response.
Relevant thermally activated transformations can include surface diffusion, phase separation or segregation, and melting.
Enhanced free-energy methods overcome the timescale limitations of standard molecular dynamics by sampling rare events.
Enhanced free-energy methods permit quantitative assessment of the free-energy landscape.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios and increased atomic fluctuations.
Higher surface-to-volume ratios and increased atomic fluctuations cause smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles to have lower phase-transition free-energy barriers than larger particles.
Decreasing nanoparticle size will decrease the transition barrier.
Lower transition barriers in smaller nanoparticles will produce earlier melting or surface segregation.
Standard molecular dynamics without enhanced free-energy sampling may fail to capture size-dependent barrier differences accurately.
The predictions are reliable only within the temperature range over which the interatomic potentials are validated.
Surface effects dominate the relevant thermal behavior for nanoparticles that are typically a few nanometers in size.
Interatomic-potential limitations and incomplete representation of atomistic processes make quantitative barrier values uncertain.
A qualitative dependence of free-energy barriers on particle size is expected despite uncertainty in their numerical values.
